items.body:
Day 2 · Chapter 2: Email

Day 2 Overview

This is the biggest chapter in the course — sending, receiving, and organizing email, the thing you'll use Outlook for every day.
Before class: instructor prep

Send each student a starter email (with a file attached) from the submission mailbox before this day begins — the Handling Incoming Messages exercises need a real message with an attachment already sitting in each student's Inbox.

Competencies Covered Today

  • Set email options
  • Send messages
  • Handle incoming messages
  • Organize messages

Today's Tasks

  1. Watch the Chapter 2 Presentation
  2. Outlook Email — read (Hands-On OU2-D1 is WebSim-only reference practice, see note below)
  3. Sending Messages — read, then complete Hands-On OU2-D2–D6
  4. Handling Incoming Messages — read, then complete Hands-On OU2-D7–D9
  5. Organizing Messages — read, then complete Hands-On OU2-D10–D15
  6. Chapter 2 Quiz (self-assessment, via eLab and Canvas)
  7. Chapter 2 Test (via eLab and Canvas)
How Hands-On grading works today

Unlike Chapter 1, today's Develop Your Skills exercises are built around WebSims (Labyrinth's simulated Outlook environment) — but WebSim completion doesn't produce a screenshot you control the way real Outlook does. Instead, you'll work live in your real VACE Outlook account and prove each exercise by sending a real email to [SUBMISSION-EMAIL-PLACEHOLDER — Josh to provide before publishing], the monitored inbox your instructor checks for completion. The WebSim link is still available below for review/practice before or after each reading.

items.title: Outlook Email — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Chapter 2 Reading

Book pages: 14-15 · Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: Set email options

Outlook Email

An email account can come from three places: your employer or school, an Internet service provider (ISP), or a webmail provider like Gmail or Outlook.com. Outlook itself doesn't create or supply an email account — it only gives you access to one you already have, using the account type, email address, and password to set it up (Outlook attempts this automatically, falling back to manual "Advanced Options" setup when needed).

An email address follows a username@domain pattern — the @ symbol separates the two. Account and email settings live in Backstage view (click the File tab); the Back button (top-left arrow) returns you to the main Outlook window.

Working with Web-Based Simulations

Most of this course's Develop Your Skills exercises are also available as web-based simulations (WebSims) — a safe, consequence-free way to practice sending/receiving/organizing mail without needing real people on the other end. Whenever you see the WebSim cloud icon, you're working as if you were using real Outlook, just on a web page instead.

Develop Your Skills OU2-D1 (setting up an email account) is WebSim-only in the book, since students don't normally have permission to create a new account on a shared computer — but since you already set up and used your real VACE Outlook account in Chapter 1, there's nothing new to submit here. The WebSim link at the end of this module is there if you want the practice/reference.

items.title: Sending Messages — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Chapter 2 Reading

Book pages: 16-25 · Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: Send messages

Sending Messages

A few netiquette rules to follow: always fill in the subject line, use correct grammar and punctuation, never type in all caps (it reads as YELLING), and never write anything in an email you wouldn't want made public.

To, Cc, and Bcc

Everyone in the To field is a primary recipient. The Cc field is for people who only need the information and aren't expected to reply. The Bcc field protects privacy — Bcc'd recipients are invisible to everyone else, and To/Cc recipients can't even tell a Bcc exists. Bcc isn't shown by default; you have to add it via the message window's Options.

{{img:pg 17.png|Textbook page 17 — an annotated message window showing From, To, Cc, Bcc, Subject, and Message fields}}

Outlook also "learns" addresses you've sent to before via the Auto Complete Email List, suggesting them as you type — a separate file from your contacts, easy to overlook when moving to a new computer.

Signatures

A signature (your name, title, company, contact info) can be appended to messages automatically. You can create multiple signatures and set different defaults for New Messages vs. Replies/Forwards — and it matters: sending a formal email with the wrong default signature attached looks unprofessional.

Attaching Files

You can attach documents, pictures, or other Outlook items — the Recent Items list under Attach File speeds this up, and drag-and-drop into the message body also works. If you type a word like "attach" or "attached" but forget to actually attach anything, Outlook shows an Attachment Reminder dialog before it lets you send.

The Spelling & Grammar Checker

Checks the message body (and appointments and Notes, not just email) against Outlook's dictionary — but it only catches words that aren't in the dictionary at all. A correctly-spelled wrong word ("Broad Meeting" instead of "Board Meeting") slips right through, so proofreading is still on you. Right-click a flagged word to fix it, Ignore/Ignore All/Add to Dictionary, or run the full checker via Review → Proofing → Spelling & Grammar (F7).

items.title: Hands-On OU2-D2–D6: Compose, Sign, Attach & Check Your Email
items.description:
Book pages: 17-26 · Develop Your Skills OU2-D2 through OU2-D6

Hands-On OU2-D2–D6: Compose, Sign, Attach & Check Your Email

Hands-On Exercise — work live in your real Outlook account
Submit to:

[SUBMISSION-EMAIL-PLACEHOLDER — Josh to provide before publishing]. Prefix every subject line with your name so they're easy to find, e.g. "Jane Doe — OU2-D2."

Part 1 — OU2-D2: Multiple Recipients

  1. Compose a new email. Address it To the submission address; Cc a classmate; Bcc yourself.
  2. Subject: "[Your Name] — OU2-D2." Write a short message explaining what the To/Cc/Bcc fields each do.
  3. Send it.

Part 2 — OU2-D3: Create Signatures

  1. Message → Signature menu → Signatures.
  2. Create two signatures: "Professional" (your name, a title, contact info) and "Casual" (a short informal sign-off).
  3. Set Professional as the default for New Messages, and pick a default for Replies/Forwards.
  4. Click Save.

Part 3 — OU2-D4: Apply a Signature

  1. Compose a new email to the submission address. Subject: "[Your Name] — OU2-D4."
  2. Manually switch the signature to your Casual one via Message → Signature menu, before sending.
  3. Send it.

Part 4 — OU2-D5: Attach a File

  1. Compose a new email to the submission address. Subject: "[Your Name] — OU2-D5."
  2. Choose Message → Attach File and attach any file (a document, image, whatever you have handy).
  3. Send it.

Part 5 — OU2-D6: Spelling & Grammar Check

  1. Compose a new email to the submission address. Subject: "[Your Name] — OU2-D6."
  2. Type a few sentences with 2-3 deliberate typos, then run Review → Spelling & Grammar (F7) and correct them before sending.
  3. Send it.

items.title: Handling Incoming Messages — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Chapter 2 Reading

Book pages: 27-34 · Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: Handle incoming messages

Handling Incoming Messages

Unread messages show up with bold blue subject text and a blue bar down the left side. You can read a message right in the Reading pane, or double-click to open it in its own window. Related messages group into conversations by subject, with an expand arrow to see the whole thread.

Saving Attachments

Word and Excel attachments open in their own app when you double-click them (a single click just previews them in Outlook). Other file types prompt an "Opening Mail Attachment" dialog. Be careful: viruses often spread through .exe attachments — always think about the file type and whether you trust the sender before opening anything.

Replying and Forwarding

Reply auto-fills the sender's address, adds "RE:" to the subject, and quotes the original message. Forward leaves the To field blank (you choose who gets it) and adds "FW:" instead. Use Reply All carefully — only when everyone on the original thread genuinely needs to see your response, not by default.

Flagging Messages

Flagging marks a message for later action and adds it to your To-Do list — options include Today, Tomorrow, This Week, Next Week, or a custom date. (Exchange accounts get more flag options than internet-based/webmail accounts.)

{{img:pg 32.png|Textbook page 32 — the flag options menu, showing the fuller set available on an Exchange account vs. the limited set on an internet-based account}}

Printing Messages

Print from Backstage view (File → Print) — Memo style prints the message with header info, Table style prints a list view. To print an attachment, open it in its native app and print from there, or right-click it and choose Quick Print.

items.title: Hands-On OU2-D7–D9: Read, Reply, Forward, Flag & Print
items.description:
Book pages: 29-34 · Develop Your Skills OU2-D7 through OU2-D9

Hands-On OU2-D7–D9: Read, Reply, Forward, Flag & Print

Hands-On Exercise — uses the starter email your instructor sent you
Before you start

Check your Inbox for a starter email from your instructor with a file attached — you'll need it for Part 1. Submit everything to [SUBMISSION-EMAIL-PLACEHOLDER — Josh to provide before publishing], subject prefixed with your name.

Part 1 — OU2-D7: Save an Attachment

  1. Open your instructor's starter email.
  2. Right-click the attachment, choose Save As, and save it somewhere you can find again.
  3. Reply to the starter email confirming you saved it, and attach the saved copy as proof.

Part 2 — OU2-D8: Reply and Forward

  1. Reply to the starter email with a one-line thank-you.
  2. Forward the same starter email to the submission address, with your own note added above the original message.

Part 3 — OU2-D9: Flag and Print

  1. Flag the starter email for follow-up (any date option).
  2. Open Backstage Print options for that message and review the Memo vs. Table style choices — you don't need to actually print.
  3. Send a final email to the submission address confirming you flagged the message and which print style you'd use and why.

items.title: Organizing Messages — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Chapter 2 Reading

Book pages: 34-43 · Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: Organize messages

Organizing Messages

You can create your own folder structure — new folders (via the Folder tab or right-click → New Folder) sort alphabetically among existing ones and can nest inside each other. The Favorites list at the top of the Folder pane can hold any folder you want quick access to, in whatever order you drag them into.

Move or copy messages into folders by dragging, right-clicking, or using Ribbon commands — Ctrl+click to select several non-adjacent messages, Shift+click for a range.

Quick Steps and Rules

Quick Steps bundle a repetitive multi-step task (like forward-then-file) into one button you click manually. Rules are different — they run automatically every time a message matches your criteria (like playing a sound or moving mail to a folder whenever it's from a specific person).

{{img:pg 38.png|Textbook page 38 — the Rules menu and the Create Rule dialog, with conditions and actions}}

Sorting, Searching, Deleting, Archiving

Messages sort by date (newest first) by default, but there are 13 sort criteria to choose from (From, Subject, Size, Importance, and more). The Search box searches your current mailbox by default and can expand to the current folder or everywhere. Deleted messages go to the Deleted Items folder and stay recoverable until you empty it (Ctrl+Z undoes an accidental delete). Archiving moves old-but-wanted messages out of your active mailbox to free up space, without deleting them — accessed via File → Tools → Clean Up Old Items, or the Move to Archive Folder button.

items.title: Hands-On OU2-D10–D15: Folders, Quick Steps, Rules, Search, Delete & Archive
items.description:
Book pages: 35-43 · Develop Your Skills OU2-D10 through OU2-D15

Hands-On OU2-D10–D15: Folders, Quick Steps, Rules, Search, Delete & Archive

Hands-On Exercise — no message to send for these, so confirm by email instead
What to submit

One email to [SUBMISSION-EMAIL-PLACEHOLDER — Josh to provide before publishing], subject "[Your Name] — OU2-D10–D15," describing what you built in each part below.

Part 1 — OU2-D10: Folders & Favorites

  1. Right-click Inbox → New Folder. Create two folders with names of your choice.
  2. Right-click one of them and choose Add to Favorites.

Part 2 — OU2-D11: Move Messages

  1. Drag one message into one of your new folders.
  2. Select two more messages (Ctrl+click) and use Home → Move → Other Folder to move them into the other new folder.

Part 3 — OU2-D12: Quick Step & Rule

  1. Home → Quick Steps → New Quick Step → Move to Folder. Name it and point it at one of your new folders.
  2. Home → More Commands → Rules → Create Rule. Set a condition (e.g. Subject contains a keyword) and an action (move to folder). Save it.

Part 4 — OU2-D13: Search

  1. Use the Search box to find a message by keyword.

Part 5 — OU2-D14: Delete

  1. Delete a message you don't need, then empty Deleted Items.

Part 6 — OU2-D15: Archive

  1. Select an old message and use the Move to Archive Folder button (or File → Tools → Clean Up Old Items).
